notes.meaning: Gaal brags to the crowd that if he were in charge, he would get rid of Abimelech. He calls out a bold challenge, telling Abimelech to gather his army and come fight. Gaal uses big talk to win over the people and make himself their new ruler.

Zebul, the governor of Shechem, hears Gaal's proud words and becomes very angry. Gaal had insulted both him and his master, Abimelech. Zebul hides his anger for the moment so he can plan a secret countermove.

Zebul secretly sends messengers to warn Abimelech about the rebellion. He reports that Gaal and his brothers have arrived in Shechem and are turning the city against him. Zebul urges Abimelech to step in before Gaal takes full control.

Zebul tells Abimelech to march his troops at night and hide in the open fields. At sunrise, he should launch a surprise attack against the city. When Gaal comes out to fight, Abimelech can strike him with full force.

Abimelech follows Zebul's advice and leads his army out under cover of darkness. He splits his troops into four separate companies and sets up an ambush near Shechem. He waits quietly for dawn to catch the rebels unprepared.

At sunrise, Gaal walks out and stands at the city gate to see what is happening. Just then, Abimelech and his men rise up from their hiding spots. Gaal does not realize at first that an entire army has surrounded the area.

Gaal spots the soldiers and tells Zebul that people are coming down from the mountaintops. Zebul tricks him by claiming those figures are only shadows cast by the mountains. This lie keeps Gaal calm and gives Abimelech's troops more time to close in.

Gaal looks again and insists that armed men really are advancing toward them. He points out one group marching from the high ground and another coming down the road by the Diviners' Oak. Now Zebul can no longer hide the truth from him.

Zebul drops his disguise and mocks Gaal for his loud boasting. He reminds Gaal of his earlier claim that Abimelech was nothing and dares him to go out and fight. Proud talk is easily silenced when real danger arrives.

Gaal leads the men of Shechem out to battle against Abimelech, but he is quickly overwhelmed. Abimelech drives him back in full retreat, and many of Gaal's men fall wounded all the way to the city gate. Gaal's bold promises crumble the moment he faces real battle.

Abimelech pulls back to the nearby town of Arumah, while Zebul drives Gaal and his family out of Shechem. The citizens are ready to abandon Gaal because his bold talk ended in total failure. Gaal leaves the city in disgrace and disappears from Scripture.

The next morning, the people of Shechem walk out into their fields, likely thinking the conflict is over and they can work in peace. Someone immediately sends word to Abimelech. He sees an easy chance to take revenge on the city that betrayed him.

Abimelech divides his soldiers into three companies and hides them in the fields. When the townspeople come out of the city, he springs the trap and attacks them. The helpless workers are caught completely by surprise.

Abimelech and his company sprint forward to block the city gate so no one can escape inside. Meanwhile, the other two companies hunt down the people scattered across the fields. Cut off from all safety, the Shechemites are struck down without mercy.

Abimelech fights against the city all day until he breaks through its defenses and kills everyone inside. He tears down the buildings and scatters salt across the ground. Spreading salt was a symbolic act showing he wanted Shechem to remain a barren ruin forever.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view verses 42–49 as a second, independent account of the attack on Shechem that was later combined with the earlier story.

notes.meaning: When the leaders in the fortified tower of Shechem hear what happened, they take refuge in the temple of their idol, El-berith. They trust that the sacred building will shield them from harm. Word quickly reaches Abimelech that all these leaders are cornered in one place.

Abimelech leads his army up Mount Zalmon and cuts down a tree branch with his axe. He hoists it onto his shoulder and tells his soldiers to do exactly what they saw him do. His men quickly copy his actions and gather their own branches.

The soldiers carry their branches to the temple stronghold and pile them against the walls. They set the pile on fire, killing about a thousand men and women inside through the flames and thick smoke. Running to a false god brings no protection against disaster.

After destroying Shechem, Abimelech marches against the neighboring town of Thebez and captures it. Thebez was an allied city that had joined in the rebellion. Abimelech continues his campaign of revenge without slowing down.

The citizens and leaders of Thebez run into a strong tower inside the city to make their final stand. They shut and bar the doors behind them and crowd onto the flat roof. They hope the stone fortress will hold out against the attackers.

Abimelech attacks the tower and marches right up to the wooden entrance to burn it down, just as he did in Shechem. His previous success makes him careless about his own safety. He steps directly under the high walls, exposing himself to danger.

A woman on the roof drops a heavy upper millstone onto Abimelech's head, cracking his skull. Abimelech had murdered his seventy brothers on a single stone, and now a stone crushes him. God uses an ordinary woman and a household tool to bring down a cruel ruler.

Knowing his wound is fatal, Abimelech quickly calls his armor-bearer to run him through with a sword. He cares more about his reputation than his soul and cannot bear the thought of people saying a woman killed him. His final act shows that his pride remained stubborn until his very last breath.

When the Israelite soldiers see that Abimelech is dead, they drop their weapons and go back to their homes. His death instantly dissolves his army and brings an end to the civil war. Without their ruthless leader, the troops have no reason to keep fighting.

In this outcome, God pays back Abimelech for the evil of murdering his seventy brothers. God also repays the men of Shechem for helping Abimelech carry out that slaughter. Everything that happens fulfills the warning curse that Jotham spoke over them.
